# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–30 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing into summer and now winter. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year).
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall (Carbury Manor House); Carbury Chase; Beccles; Quenwick; Harrowgate; Dunwick; Liverpool; San Francisco; California; Salt Lake City; New Mexico; Arizona; Mexico; Vera Cruz; Queenstown; Langham Hotel; Euston Square Railway Station.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (appointed administratrix). All other property in valueless shares.
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc (Chapters 27–30)
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, falsely claiming virtuous past. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Within week, Jos became her "entirely slave." Changed habits; praised Dobbin constantly to Emmy; told her she behaved cruelly toward him. Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner with adjacent suite, carriage, entertainments.

**Dobbin's Opposition and Departure**: Called her "the little minx"; stormed at Jos. Amelia embraced Becky warmly and flung Dobbin an angry, scornful glance—the most unjust of her life. **Dobbin had spent fifteen years devoted to Amelia; she grew accustomed to trampling on him but did not wish to marry him—only to keep him.** Dobbin departed with haughty bow.

**Insurance and Death**: Jos effected heavy insurance; Dobbin procured prolonged leave, went alarmed. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged payment; Rebecca dared them to refuse, declared herself victim of "infamous conspiracy." Solicitors Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes triumphed; £2,000 paid, split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix). **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication with Rebecca.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declined to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in works of piety, church attendance with footman, appears on all Charity Lists, has stalls at Fancy Fairs.

## Amelia and William Dobbin's Resolution (Chapter 29)
**Becky's Revelation**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy...who had neither wit, nor manners, nor heart." Produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot." **"Dobbin forced him to keep his word."**

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy wept; internal struggle: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present at ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child; they became great friends.

## Supporting Characters—Old
- **Glorvina O'Dowd**: Married Major Posky after his first wife's death. Colonel Sir Michael O'Dowd advanced to Major-General; Lady O'Dowd lives in "great splendour at O'Dowdstown."
- **George Osborne (son)**: "Dashing young gentleman"; hunted and shot with Rawdon; at Cambridge; quarrelled with Rawdon over Lady Jane's daughter.
- **Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.** (young baronet): Lives at Queen's Crawley with Lady Jane and daughter; declined to see mother Rebecca.

## Lady Carbury and Family (Chapter 30)
**Character**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. **"The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was."** Devoted to children, especially Felix. No ambition to write good books; painfully anxious to write ones critics would praise through inducing their commendation.

**Workspace**: Back drawing-room (divided by permanently closed doors) is workspace for writing books and contriving systems to inveigle editors and critics.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him as boy and man; almost proud of his vices. Philosophy: "carpe diem." Possesses two unpaid-for horses. Demands money from mother to maintain appearance in Grosvenor Square. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming (still retains winnings). **Currently considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); at Melmotte ball, waltzes with Marie and studies words as lesson ("I do"), repeating them to convince poor girl he could love her.** Left ball early to Beargarden—gambling devil hot within him. **Since Roger's offer to Henrietta, Felix has "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment."** Despite debts, claims to be "all right"; boasts money in pocket and that others owe him money. Roger suspects talk of giving home for Henrietta is delusional. Felix lacks courage to shake off Roger violently and will not be "sat upon" by him, yet dreads Roger's words with "craven fear."

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance commenced. Cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, nearly forty) passionately in love with her. Paul Montague is another gentleman whom Henrietta has seen. Roger offered hand in marriage with declaration: "Very serious to me. I may say so serious that nothing in my own life can approach it in importance." **Paul Montague fell into love with Henrietta during second visit to Carbury Hall; "great harm had come of it."** Scene between Roger and Paul lasted above an hour with very hot words. Paul packed clothes and was driven by Roger to railway station without seeing either lady, departing in tears. Roger blessed him at platform: "God bless you, old fellow." **Henrietta rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young to marry and age disparity insurmountable; admitted "even that disparity was not now her strongest reason for feeling sure that she could not marry Roger Carbury."** Within week, Paul Montague returned "as a still dear friend," having promised not to see Henrietta again for three months but nothing further. Paul argued to Roger: "If she won't take you, there is no reason why I shouldn't try." Paul questioned why Roger should be "a dog in the manger"; believed he could yield if Roger could make anything of his offer. Though Paul doubted his finances (share in "doubtful business of Fisker, Montague, and Montague, in a wretched little town 250 miles further off than San Francisco"), he declared he had money and would not give up Henrietta on account of finances. Roger would not accede to justice of Paul's argument, believing Paul bound to retire from lack of income, prior claim, and gratitude.

**Lady Carbury's Divided Concerns**: Solicitude for son greatly increases desire for daughter's union with Roger. If daughter could be settled, Lady Carbury said to herself, she could devote herself to Felix's interests. However, she paid so much for Felix and would have so much more extracted that she might be unable to keep home for daughter. Roger came to London to address "the indispensable necessity...of taking some steps by which at any rate the young man's present expenses might be brought to an end." Roger horrified that man with no income has hunters. Roger recommended Lady Carbury give up house in town, find home for daughter elsewhere, let Felix "bear the brunt of his own misdoings." Roger spoke severely of Felix; Lady Carbury mentioned notes and gold on Felix's table, suggesting gambling winnings. Roger declared: "I can understand that you should provide him with bed and food, but not that you should pander to his vices by giving him money." **Roger believes remedy lies in mother's conduct: were she not foolishly weak, she would divide utterly from son and leave him to suffer utter penury, which would bring him round.** At present, Felix has money and will eat and drink of best, free from inconvenience. **Roger fired last shot: "You will ruin your sister, and break your mother's heart." He took money as certain gambling proceeds.** Roger resolved to warn Henrietta against Melmotte connection and advised her to regard him as elder brother. Henrietta resented implication that Roger might think Melmotte connection could affect his own interests. Roger confessed his only wish is "to travel the same road with you" and that "No contact with legions of Melmottes could make you other to me than the woman on whom my heart has settled...I love you so well that I have already taken you for better or for worse. I cannot change." He asked: "Have you a word to say to comfort me?" When he spoke of walking Carbury shrubberies asking "what chance there is of your walking there as the mistress," Henrietta put out her hand and allowed it to remain in his for a moment, but turned away without answering. **Roger remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds to old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile."** Old-fashioned notion that success condonation had never reached him. He would feel himself disgraced to enter house of Augustus Melmotte. "Not all the duchesses in the peerage, or all the money in the city, could alter his notions or induce him to modify his conduct." He trusted Henrietta had "higher turn of mind than her mother" and remained "kept free from soil." As for Felix, "he had so grovelled in the gutters as to be dirt all over. Nothing short of the prolonged sufferings of half a life could cleanse him."

## The Melmottes (Chapter 30)
**Augustus Melmotte, Esq.**: Arrived in London from Paris within last two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks native language fluently with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money,--though his character was perhaps worth but little." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair, expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face; repellent unless attracted by internal consideration. Magnificent in expenditure, powerful in doings, successful in business; world not repelled. **Miles Grendall serves as his usher/secretary in his office.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Said to have been Bohemian Jewess; admits to being foreigner, speaks very little English. Birthplace of daughter disputed: some say New York; Madame declares Paris.

**Marie Melmotte**: Spoke as Mademoiselle Marie; now speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough** (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered). Had experience with Lord Nidderdale, who half-laughingly said he "might just as well take her for his wife." Now contemplating own happiness. **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.** Roger considers Melmotte connection "absolutely disgraceful. A social connection with the first crossing-sweeper would be less objectionable."

**Melmotte Wealth**: As affairs prospered, immediate disposition of Marie became less necessary; Melmotte reduced offers for suitors. Visible wealth certain: house, furniture, carriages, horses, servants with livery and powdered heads, gems, presents. Two dinner parties daily. Tradesmen "quite free of doubt"; "money in daily use" evident.

## Roger Carbury of Carbury Hall (Chapter 30)
**Character and Standing**: Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father before him likewise. Orders to Beccles tradesmen not extensive; care taken goods neither overcharged nor unnecessary. Tradesmen consequently did not care much for him, though elders entertained ancient reverence for family. "Carbury of Carbury"—distinction of itself. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase (partly in Carbury parish, partly Bundlesham) belongs unfortunately in entirety to Bundlesham estate.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme (Chapter 30 – NEW)
**The Enterprise**: Grand proposal for railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through fertile lands of New Mexico and Arizona into Mexican Republic, running by city of Mexico, terminating at Gulf port of Vera Cruz. **Distance approximately 2,000 miles; no computation made as to probable cost.** Fisker considers such questions "beside the mark and childish."

**Government Support and Infrastructure**: Concession obtained from United States Government through territories; correspondence maintained with President of Mexican Republic. Claim made of office already open in Mexico and another at Vera Cruz.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock to be taken "at par"; shares to be sold at premium. Goal to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum; Fisker believes better results achievable.

**Key Players**:
- **Hamilton K. Fisker**: American, age approximately forty. Partner in firm Fisker, Montague, and Montague (San Francisco). Small, shining man with well-twisted moustache, greasy brown hair becoming bald at top. Good-looking features but insignificant appearance. Gorgeously dressed with silk waistcoat, chains, carries little stick. Troubled by no shyness, scruples, or fears. Mind not capacious but his own; knows how to use it. Previously engaged in California financing. Supremely confident, good-humoured, audacious, clever. Successfully talked Paul Montague into agreeing to flour-mill at Fiskerville in California.

- **Paul Montague**: Junior member of Fisker, Montague, and Montague. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but finds himself unable to resist the man's combination of good humour, audacity, and cleverness. Trembles for his money and wishes never to see Fisker again; yet when Fisker came to England, felt proud to remember Fisker was his partner. Obeyed Fisker's telegram order (sent on shore at Queenstown from New York liner) to meet at Liverpool immediately. Met with Fisker at great railway hotel at Liverpool, where Fisker displayed maps, schedules, printed programmes. Fisker convinced Paul (with doubt and dismay) to write letter inviting Melmotte to meet Fisker and discuss the railway scheme. Paul recopied letter at Liverpool, signed it, stating Fisker's eagerness to see Melmotte and assurance of Melmotte's desirability as co-operator. Letter dated from Langham Hotel, posted at Euston Square Railway Station upon Fisker's arrival. **Following morning, Paul and Fisker travelled to London together.** Fisker presented himself in Abchurch Lane; letter resulted in twenty-minute wait before audience with Melmotte granted.

**Targeting Melmotte**: Fisker convinced Paul that if Melmotte "goes in for the thing" he would "be one of us," enabling partnership without need for borrowing. Fisker asserts Melmotte would see way to making couple of million dollars from the scheme. Fisker emphasizes Americans "go after bigger things" than Europeans, suggesting Melmotte "pretty nigh beats the best among us" and should "come and try his luck." Fisker claims Melmotte is "safe thing" because of his proven financing success in Europe; Fisker believes half-hour conversation would convince Melmotte of scheme's merit.

## Minor Characters
- **Feten Lindner, Eldette Corrett, Jotho Corrett, Cotho, Maric Lindson, Nynelle Stenworth, Nynelle Stenworth (duplicate), Cotho Hollwood, Halan Hollwood, Rira Stenworth, Orric, Jovus, Pebin Wexwood, Orric Wexwood**: Inhabitants of rural hill farms (Coldcombe, Harrowgate, Dunwick, Quenwick, Beccles areas). Daily activities include mundane farm work, shopping, casual conversation about weather, harvests, lame horses, commodity prices (salt, oats). Eldette moved from Quenwick to Coldcombe with single trunk; Jotho Corrett followed within month. **No clear narrative function; appear as ambient rural life details.**
